problem: P if and only if Q. Q if and only if R. Not R. Conclusion: not P. Does the conclusion necessarily follow from the premises? Answer Yes or No.

answer.raw:
Step 1: Given "P if and only if Q," we can write this as P ↔ Q.
Step 2: Given "Q if and only if R," we can write this as Q ↔ R.
Step 3: Given "Not R," we have ¬R.
Step 4: From Q ↔ R and ¬R, we can infer ¬Q (since Q and R are equivalent, if R is false, Q must also be false).
Step 5: From P ↔ Q and ¬Q, we can infer ¬P (since P and Q are equivalent, if Q is false, P must also be false).
Step 6: The conclusion "not P" follows logically from the premises.

FINAL ANSWER: Yes

  | (push Not; intros; simp_all; decide; done)

theorem s1_wf : P ↔ Q := by sorry
theorem s1_pos : P ↔ Q := by fv_auto
theorem s1_neg : ¬ (P ↔ Q) := by fv_auto

theorem s2_wf : Q ↔ R := by sorry
theorem s2_pos : Q ↔ R := by fv_auto
theorem s2_neg : ¬ (Q ↔ R) := by fv_auto

theorem s3_wf : ¬R := by sorry
theorem s3_pos : ¬R := by fv_auto
theorem s3_neg : ¬ (¬R) := by fv_auto

theorem s4_wf : (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬Q := by sorry
theorem s4_pos : (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬Q := by fv_auto
theorem s4_neg : ¬ ((Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬Q) := by fv_auto

theorem s5_wf : (P ↔ Q) → ¬Q → ¬P := by sorry
theorem s5_pos : (P ↔ Q) → ¬Q → ¬P := by fv_auto
theorem s5_neg : ¬ ((P ↔ Q) → ¬Q → ¬P) := by fv_auto

theorem s6_wf : ∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P := by sorry
theorem s6_pos : ∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P := by fv_auto
theorem s6_neg : ¬ (∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P) := by fv_auto

theorem final_wf : ∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P := by sorry
theorem final_pos : ∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P := by fv_auto
theorem final_neg : ¬ (∀ (P Q R : Prop), (P ↔ Q) → (Q ↔ R) → ¬R → ¬P) := by fv_auto
